passage: In her hostel room in Bengaluru, Shalini drew the chain on a sheet: 'Job at a product company' at the top, and beneath it 'crack the final interview', then 'clear the online test', then 'strong project on my resume'. Neat arrows all the way down. She showed it to Lalit, a classmate. 'What's the first box?' he asked. She pointed at the bottom one: 'Get better at coding.' 'Better how? By when? With what?' She shrugged; the arrows looked so tidy she had never asked. Weeks went by. The sheet stayed on the wall and she felt organised, but her practice was scattered, a few videos here, a few problems there. At the online test in October she found she had never checked whether two months was enough. She fell short.

qa.q: How might Lalit see her chart?
qa.a: Lalit probably sees a tidy chart with a vague base, which is why he asked how, by when and with what.

"Product company, associate role, by next July," Rajni said, pointing at her notebook in the canteen. "Working back: offer in May, interviews March, shortlist in January, portfolio by December, internship this summer."
Lalit read it. "That's really neat. What's the first step?"
"Build skills."
"Which skills?"
"You know. Design thinking. Some data. Product sense."
"And this week?"
Rajni laughed. "This week I'm doing the plan."
Two months later, the summer internship list came out. Every listing asked for a small case study or a project link.
Lalit found her by the notice board. "Do you have anything to send?"
Rajni stared at the list. "I have a very good plan." Her voice cracked. "I don't have a single project."
"Let's pick one this weekend," Lalit said. "One. Small."

qa.q: When did the summer internship list come out?
qa.a: It came out two months later.

qa.q: What was Rajni feeling when her voice cracked at the notice board?
qa.a: She was shocked and ashamed, realising her neat plan had never produced a single project to send.

qa.q: What would you change first in Rajni's plan?
qa.a: I would turn "build skills" into one small project with a date this week, since every later step depends on having something to show.

qa.q: How does Lalit see Rajni's plan from the start?
qa.a: Lalit sees it looks tidy but notices the first step is vague, which is why Lalit keeps asking "which skills" and "this week".

grounding: It shows a final-year student whose backward plan to a product-company job looks neat while its first step stays vague, costing an internship chance.

I'm Lalremsiami, and last year I had the most beautiful career plan in my hostel.
Goal: analyst at a product company. Before that: pass the case interview. Before that: get shortlisted. Before that: a strong resume. Before that: "get good at SQL and statistics." I drew it as a staircase on chart paper and stuck it above my bed. Noor, my roommate, said it looked like a poster from a coaching centre.
Every step had a date except the bottom one. "Get good" never became a course, a book or a number of hours. I kept polishing the top steps, reading interview tips, practising my introduction.
In October the campus test had forty minutes of SQL. I solved two of eight questions.
Now when I plan backwards, I stop at the bottom and ask: what, exactly, will I do tomorrow morning?

qa.q: How many SQL questions did Lalremsiami solve in the campus test?
qa.a: Lalremsiami solved two of eight questions.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami probably feel after the October test?
qa.a: Lalremsiami probably felt crushed and foolish, since the plan had looked beautiful but the one vague step was exactly what the test checked.

qa.q: What else could Lalremsiami have done with the bottom step, and why?
qa.a: The bottom step could have become a specific course with weekly hours, so progress could be seen long before October.

qa.q: How might Noor have seen the staircase above the bed?
qa.a: Noor saw it as a neat poster, which suggests it looked impressive from outside while the real work had not started.

grounding: It shows a final-year student whose tidy backward chain to a product-company job hides a vague first step, which costs them in the campus test.
